newsitem.title: UK: Laird to push expansion despite sterling.
newsitem.headline: Laird to push expansion despite sterling.

text.p: Engineering company Laird Group Plc said on Thursday that it would continue its expansion plans in the current year despite high start-up costs and strength of the sterling, which had recently affected its overseas profits.
Laird, which announced a marginal rise in its 1996 pretax profits to 69.2 million stg also said earnings in the first two months of 1997 has been ahead of the previous year.

"The group has the financial and management resources to support its continuing development, while the geographic and commercial spread of its multinational businesses provide a strong base from which to continue to take advantage of opportunities for growth," Laird said.
The sterling strength in 1996 reduced the value of its overseas net assets by 33 million stg, after it increased by 16 million in 1995. Overseas profits fell by 0.6 million stg.
The company, however, said it would continue its plans to increase its international operations of its automobile operations and expand its overall non-automotive business.
The group's 1996 profits were based on a turnover of 973.9 million stg and inspired by 25 percent growth in its non-auto businesses in 1996.
The non-auto businesses, mainly security systems, computer components and plastics, has trebled in the past four years, increasing from under a quarter of its group profits to more than half.

Laird is setting up a car body seal plant in North Carolina which would feed the North American market. Over $50 million would be invested in the project, with the first phase due for completion in late 1997.
It is also expanding its sealing systems division in France where it recently invested four million stg to cater to fresh orders including a new Clio model of Renault to be launched in 1998..
The company said it was confident with its financial base, which it felt was sound enough to meet its long-term strategies.
"The strong cash flow reduced net borrowings at the year end to less than three percent of shareholders funds. The financial planning for the future is well in hand," it said.
